p.src: The marks already on the board may look a little like the Schrödinger equation, but that is not tonight’s subject. The subject is symmetry and conservation. There is no honest way to explain their connection without equations. The equations are elementary; what matters is arranging them so that the structure becomes visible. Scientific American may name the result, but here we want the minimum mathematics required to derive it as physicists would.

Introduce a small parameter $\epsilon$. We retain terms proportional to $\epsilon$ and discard $O(\epsilon^2)$. This is shorthand for a limiting argument, not a claim that a nonzero real number literally has zero square. For an ordinary function $f(x,y)$, $\delta f
  =\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\delta x
   +\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,\delta y
   +O(\epsilon^2),$ where both $\delta x$ and $\delta y$ are proportional to $\epsilon$. The symbol $\delta f$ means the change in $f$, not the product of a number called $\delta$ with $f$. A stationary point obeys $\delta f=0
  \qquad\hbox{to first order.}$

p.src:
For a mechanical path $q_i(t)$, the analogous quantity is the action $S[q]=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt.$ Varying the path while fixing its endpoints gives $\delta S
  =\int_{t_1}^{t_2}dt\,
   \sum_i\left(
     \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}\,\delta q_i
     +\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}\,\delta\dot q_i
   \right).$ The two terms arise because changing a path changes both its position and its velocity. Integration by parts, together with $\delta q_i(t_1)=\delta q_i(t_2)=0$, turns $\delta S=0$ into $\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}\right)
  -\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}=0.$

p.src: Cartesian positions are too narrow a language for general mechanics. The coordinates may be particle positions, angles, collective variables, or field amplitudes, so we call them $q_i$. A Lagrangian is a compressed specification of the dynamics. Even the Standard Model, written out without very condensed notation, occupies roughly a page; writing a separate equation of motion for every field component would occupy vastly more. The one function $L$ packages all of them.

p.src: Begin with a free particle of unit mass, $L=\frac{\dot q^2}{2}.$ Translate every point of its history by the same constant: $q'(t)=q(t)+\epsilon.$ Since $\epsilon$ is time independent, $\dot q'=\dot q$, and therefore $\delta L=0$. This invariance is translation symmetry.

p.src:
Consider one particle in the plane, $L=\frac{m}{2}(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)-V(x^2+y^2).$ This is a central potential. We compare two fixed coordinate systems rotated relative to one another; the axes are not rotating in time. With one consistent orientation, $\begin{aligned}
  x'&=x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta,
  \notag\\
  y'&=-x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta.
  \end{aligned}$

p.src:
Unlike a translation, the amount by which $x$ changes depends on $y$, and the amount by which $y$ changes depends on $x$. Nevertheless, $\begin{aligned}
  \delta(x^2+y^2)
  &=2x\,\delta x+2y\,\delta y=0,
  \notag\\
  \delta(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)
  &=2\dot x\,\delta\dot x+2\dot y\,\delta\dot y=0.
  \end{aligned}$ Both the potential and kinetic terms are invariant.

p.src:
Now restrict attention to a physical path, so the Euler–Lagrange equations hold. Using $\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}=p_i,
  \qquad
  \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}=\dot p_i,$ we find $\begin{aligned}
  \delta L
  &=\sum_i\left(\dot p_i\,\delta q_i
                +p_i\,\delta\dot q_i\right)
  \notag\\
  &=\frac{d}{dt}\sum_i p_i\delta q_i
  =\epsilon\frac{d}{dt}\sum_i p_i f_i(q).
  \end{aligned}$ The central step is only the product rule.

p.src: The examples now cease to be accidents. A common translation has $f_1=f_2=1$, so $\mathcal Q=p_1+p_2.$ The asymmetric translation has $f_1=B$, $f_2=-A$, so $\mathcal Q=Bp_1-Ap_2.$ For rotation, $f_x=y$ and $f_y=-x$: $\mathcal Q=p_xy-p_yx.$ Up to the orientation sign, this is angular momentum, $J=xp_y-yp_x.$

p.src: The Harmonic Oscillator in Phase Space

u.src: The Harmonic Oscillator in Phase Space
en: The Harmonic Oscillator in Phase Space

p.src:
With mass and spring constant set to one, $L=\frac{\dot q^2}{2}-\frac{q^2}{2}.$ The conjugate momentum and equation of motion give $p=\dot q,
  \qquad
  \dot p=-q,$ or $\dot q=p,
  \qquad
  \dot p=-q.$ These equations describe uniform circular motion in the $q$-$p$ plane. The back-and-forth real-space oscillator is the projection of that circle onto the $q$-axis: speed is largest at $q=0$ and vanishes at the turning points.
